summary: Gives guidance to IANA on assigning IPv4 multicast addresses. It is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 5771.

eli5.summary: It tells the address librarian how to hand out group-mailing addresses.

questions: how does administratively scoped multicast work
subtitle: How IANA assigns IPv4 addresses for group messaging

tldr.problem: IPv4 multicast addresses (for sending one message to multiple recipients) are a limited resource, and there are many different ways to use them, each needing different allocation rules.
tldr.mechanism: This document divides the multicast address space into blocks with different purposes: some for local network control, some for Internet-wide control, and others for dynamic allocation or specific protocols like GLOP and SSM.
tldr.outcome: It preserves the multicast address space by reserving blocks for dynamic allocation methods and limiting static IANA assignments.

today: RFC 5771 obsoletes this document with updated guidelines for IPv4 multicast address assignments, reflecting changes in the multicast ecosystem and allocation practices.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Multicast is a way to send a single message to multiple recipients at once, like a group text message instead of individual ones. Each multicast group has an IPv4 address, and when someone sends to that address, all computers listening to that group receive the message.

Because the IPv4 multicast address space is much smaller than the unicast space (regular one-to-one addresses), assignments must be managed carefully. This RFC codifies IANA's practice for assigning multicast addresses, replacing informal procedures with explicit guidelines. It recommends that IANA only assign addresses in cases where dynamic methods (which don't require central assignment) cannot be used.
sections.eli5: Multicast is like a radio station: one broadcast, many listeners. There are only so many frequency channels, so the address librarian needs rules about who gets a channel.

sections.title: The Multicast Address Space
sections.content:
The IPv4 multicast address range (224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255) is divided into blocks, each serving a different purpose. The Local Network Control Block (224.0.0/24) contains addresses like 224.0.0.5 (OSPF routers), used only on the local network link and not forwarded by routers. The Internetwork Control Block (224.0.1/24) contains addresses like 224.0.1.1 (NTP) that are forwarded across the Internet.

The AD-HOC Block (224.0.2.0 through 224.0.255.0) is for applications that don't fit other categories. The Source Specific Multicast Block (232/8) is for SSM, where receivers only get traffic from explicitly chosen senders. The GLOP Block (233/8) uses a clever algorithm: a company's autonomous system number is encoded into the address, making addresses algorithmically available without central assignment. The Administratively Scoped Block (239/8) is for local use within organizations. Several other blocks are reserved for future use.
sections.eli5: The multicast address space is divided into neighborhoods. Some are for talking to neighbors on the same link. Some are for talking across the Internet. Some let companies make their own addresses using a formula.

sections.title: How Addresses Are Assigned
sections.content:
For the Local Network Control Block and Internetwork Control Block, new assignments require Expert Review, IESG Approval, or Standards Action. These blocks are reserved for protocol control traffic, and assigning one requires justifying why the application cannot use other methods.

For the AD-HOC Block, the RFC strongly discourages new assignments; IANA should only assign when dynamic methods fail. For SDP/SAP (Session Announcement Protocol), addresses are chosen randomly by users, so no IANA assignment policy is needed. For SSM and GLOP, addresses are algorithmically or dynamically assigned, eliminating the need for centralized allocation. The Administratively Scoped Block requires no IANA assignment since addresses are for local use.
sections.eli5: Some addresses need permission from IANA. Some can be picked by users. Some are calculated automatically. The RFC says to use the automatic methods first.

sections.title: Relative Offsets and Annual Reviews
sections.content:
Within the Administratively Scoped Block, there are special relative offsets: fixed addresses that represent services like session announcement. Since only 256 offsets exist, IANA should assign them only to services providing infrastructure support. New relative offset assignments require Expert Review, IESG Approval, or Standards Action.

The RFC recommends that IANA conduct annual reviews of multicast address assignments, reclaiming addresses that were mis-assigned or are no longer in use. Addresses in the AD-HOC, DIS Transient, and ST Multicast blocks should be reclaimed if they are unused on the global Internet or could instead use SSM, GLOP, or Administratively Scoped addressing.
sections.eli5: Sometimes IANA hands out addresses that don't get used. Once a year, IANA should check and take back addresses from apps that aren't using them or should have picked a different way.

sections.title: Avoiding Misuse and Interoperability
sections.content:
The RFC notes that applications MUST NOT use addressing in the IANA reserved blocks. The assignment guidelines do not alter the underlying security properties of multicast; they simply organize how addresses are distributed. The guidelines protect interoperability by ensuring different applications do not accidentally use the same address and by preventing applications from consuming the scarce static address pool unnecessarily.

By promoting dynamic allocation methods, the RFC reduces contention and simplifies the process for applications that need multicast addressing, while centralizing IANA review on only the most critical cases (control protocols that cannot use dynamic allocation).
sections.eli5: The main risk is apps fighting over addresses or wasting rare addresses on things that could pick their own. These rules help prevent that.
